title: The Effect of State Policies on the Location of Manufacturing: Evidence from State Borders
research_question: Do state-level policies that are favorable versus unfavorable to business meaningfully affect where manufacturing activity locates within the United States? In particular, does crossing from a state with a less business-friendly policy environment into one with a more business-friendly environment produce a discrete change in the level of manufacturing activity, and how large is this effect on manufacturing's share of local employment?
data_description: The analysis uses U.S. Census Bureau county-level data on manufacturing employment and total employment for the 3,078 counties of the 48 contiguous states. The county is the unit of observation. The author obtains the longitude and latitude of each county's population centroid and computes the minimum distance from each county centroid to the nearest segment of the relevant state border, retaining counties within 25 miles of that border. In addition to employment levels in the postwar period, the paper examines manufacturing employment growth rates over 1947–92. Supplementary data include the Fantus Consulting ranking of state business climates (based on 15 policy characteristics) and information on the size distribution of manufacturing establishments. State policy is classified primarily by whether a state has a right-to-work law, with passage dates ranging from 1944 (Florida, Arkansas) through 1986 (Idaho).
institutional_context: The setting is the long-running U.S. policy debate over whether state-level pro-business measures—right-to-work laws, low capital taxes, lighter environmental and safety regulation, and subsidies for new plants—attract manufacturing. Beginning with Florida and Arkansas in 1944, southern and Plains states adopted right-to-work laws (banning the union shop), and most of these same states pursued additional pro-business measures, while New England, mid-Atlantic, Great Lakes, and Pacific states generally did not. Over the postwar period, manufacturing employment grew rapidly in right-to-work states and stagnated elsewhere, but these states also differed in climate, agricultural restructuring, transportation changes, air conditioning, and union sentiment, making it hard to isolate the role of policy. The map of state borders separating these two groups of states provides paired locations whose underlying geographic conditions are similar but whose policy regimes change discretely at the state line.
